questions.question: You are researching the hospitality industry. Describe the types of businesses within the industry, and review one professional body that represents it.
questions.model_answer: answer as a short headed research summary, because Paper 2-A rewards the document format asked for. Business types: commercial businesses (hotels, restaurants, pubs) run for profit, and public sector catering (schools, colleges, hospitals) funded by government. Professional body, per the mark scheme: the Institute of Hospitality, which monitors and maintains standards, reviews CPD for its members, and liaises with the industry on best practice. Ownership types (sole trader, partnership, franchise, LLP) from Lesson 2 also earn credit in this scenario.

questions.question: Amir manages a small hotel. Tonight he expects a business traveller, a family with a baby, and a guest who uses a wheelchair. Explain how Amir should prepare to meet the needs of each customer.
questions.model_answer: Use SCAN for each guest, briefly: Spot the need, Cite the theory (customer types have differing needs), Apply it to Amir's hotel, Name the outcome. Model answer (first guest): The business traveller's main needs are speed and work facilities (Spot). The syllabus says different customer types have different needs (Cite). Amir should confirm the Wi-Fi works, offer an early breakfast and a quiet room (Apply). The guest works without stress and books again on his next trip (Name the outcome). (Repeat the same shape for the family: high chair, children's menu, safe family room; and the wheelchair user: ramp access, accessible room and toilet, staff offering help.)

questions.question: Sisters Neha and Alina want to open a café together. They are choosing between an ordinary partnership and an LLP. Using your knowledge of both business types, advise the sisters which to choose.
questions.model_answer: Use SCAN. Spot their situation (two owners, personal risk), Cite both business types with their key features, Apply each to the sisters, Name the outcome with a clear judgement. The judgement mark is real: end with "I would advise..." Model answer ending: I would advise the LLP. The extra paperwork and cost are a fair price, because if the café fails the sisters lose only what they invested, and their family homes stay protected.

questions.question: Komal's banquet hall hosts a large wedding. Her caterer's vegetable supplier delivers three hours late, so dinner is served cold and guests complain online about the HALL. Explain, using the idea of inter-relationships, why Komal was harmed by a business she never hired, and what she should do before her next event.
questions.model_answer: SCAN. Spot the chain: supplier then caterer then hall. Cite the theory: hospitality businesses depend on each other, and if one link fails the whole customer experience suffers. Apply: guests met the hall, not the supplier, so the blame lands on the customer-facing business. Name the outcome and fix: Komal should agree backup suppliers with her caterer, build relationships with nearby businesses, and confirm deliveries on the morning of every event, so one broken link cannot sink the chain again.

questions.question: Fahad's seaside guest house was full every summer. This year a recession hit, a rival guest house opened, and a rainy season kept tourists away. Fahad has also not trained his staff for two years and his online reviews mention slow service. Assess which of Fahad's problems he can control, and what he should do.
questions.model_answer: SCAN, and the sorting IS the assessment. Spot both kinds of problem. Cite the internal/external split. Apply: recession, rival, weather = external, he cannot remove them; staff training and slow service = internal, fully in his control. Name the outcome: by retraining staff and improving service quality he improves reviews and reputation, so when tourists return, they choose him over the rival. A one-line judgement earns the top mark: "Fahad should pour his energy into the internal factors, because they are the only ones he can change."

questions.question: The tourism board asks you, a hotel manager, for a short briefing paper titled "Why our industry matters to the economy". Using the five contributions to GDP, write the key points of your briefing.
questions.model_answer: Paper 2-A rewards the FORMAT asked for, so answer as a short headed briefing with five bullet points, one per contribution: sales revenue (value of meals and rooms sold), employment (wages spent back into the economy), tourism (foreign visitors' spending acts as an export), taxes (VAT, business rates and income tax fund public services), and the supply chain (hospitality's buying keeps farmers, laundries and other firms in business). One line of mechanism per bullet turns a list into full marks.

questions.question: Produce a guidance document for new colleagues summarising: (i) two allergen ingredients and one way to raise allergen awareness, and (ii) how staff assist customers with mobility issues and hearing difficulties.
questions.model_answer: answer as a headed guidance document, because Paper 2-A marks the format asked for. Mark-scheme content: (i) allergens come from the FSA's regulatory list of 14 foodstuffs; name two such as gluten, shellfish or mustard; raise awareness with an allergen factsheet shared online or on social media, plus staff training. (ii) Mobility: dedicated entry points and ramps, with access information on the website and social media so support can be requested ahead of time. Hearing: hearing loops at reception desks and entry and exit points. Close with the outcome: every guest is served safely and with dignity, and the business meets its legal duties.

questions.question: A customer at The Olive Tree restaurant tells her waiter, Salim, that she has a severe shellfish allergy. Salim thinks the chicken dish she ordered "probably" contains no shellfish, so he sends the order without comment. Explain the mistakes Salim has made and describe the correct procedure he should have followed.
questions.model_answer: Use SCAN fully; the marks are split roughly half for mistakes, half for correct procedure. Model answer: Salim's mistake is guessing about an allergen (Spot). Allergies can be life-threatening, and the rule is never guess, always check (Cite). He should have recorded the allergy on the order, told the kitchen directly, asked the chef to confirm every ingredient, and ensured separate equipment to prevent cross-contamination (Apply). Because he did none of this, the customer could suffer a severe or fatal reaction, and the business could face prosecution and permanent damage to its reputation (Name the outcome).

questions.question: The Sunrise Hotel gets excellent reviews on weekdays but poor reviews at weekends, when casual staff work without briefings or training. The owner wants to delete the bad reviews. Advise the owner on a better response, and explain how she can raise weekend service to the weekday standard.
questions.model_answer: SCAN. Spot: inconsistent service caused by untrained, unbriefed weekend staff. Cite: feedback is a free improvement plan; consistency comes from SOPs, training and briefings. Apply: reply professionally to reviews instead of deleting; introduce weekend briefings, SOPs and training for casual staff. Name the outcome: consistent standards every day, better reviews, returning guests. Finish with a judgement sentence: deleting reviews hides the symptom; training removes the cause.

questions.question: You are head waiter at Karavan Grill. Produce a one-page induction sheet for new casual staff with three headed sections: (i) the daily pre- service briefing and why attendance is compulsory, (ii) following the restaurant's SOPs, and (iii) communicating with the kitchen before making promises to guests.
questions.model_answer: Paper 2-A marks the document shape, so write a titled sheet with the three headings asked for, bullets under each. (i) Briefing: held before every service; covers today's menu changes, allergy alerts, VIPs and bookings; compulsory because every member of staff must give guests the same accurate information. (ii) SOPs: written procedures and recipe cards mean each task is done the same correct way on every shift, whoever is working; check your work against them. (iii) Kitchen communication: never promise a dish, a timing or a change the kitchen has not confirmed, because a promise made at the table is kept or broken in the kitchen. Close with the outcome: the same high standard for every customer, every time, and reviews that say so.

questions.question: As team leader, produce a maximum of two training slides: ways to encourage positive working relationships, and the benefits to the business of positive teams.
questions.model_answer: if the scenario asks for two slides, answer as two slide-shaped bullet lists; the mark scheme mirrors the requested document. Slide 1 (mark-scheme favourites): getting-to-know-you sessions, trust-building activities, mixing staff across shifts, reward programmes, regular team meetings, mentoring and shadowing for new staff. Slide 2: a happy working environment, a professional image presented to customers, trust and respect within the team, increased sales, and bonus or promotion prospects for staff. Note the extras the mark scheme loves that students forget: mixing shifts, reward programmes, mentoring and shadowing.

questions.question: At the Bluewater Hotel, staff work in silence, new employees are left to "figure things out", and good work is never acknowledged. Staff keep leaving, and recruiting replacements is costing the hotel heavily. Explain how the manager could encourage positive working relationships, and describe the benefits this would bring to the business.
questions.model_answer: SCAN. Spot: poor communication, no induction support, no recognition, high turnover. Cite: ways to encourage positive relationships (briefings, praise, sharing knowledge, fair management). Apply: introduce daily briefings, pair new staff with experienced mentors, thank and praise good work, hold occasional team events. Name the outcome: motivated staff stay longer, cutting recruitment costs, and coordinated teams give better service, bringing repeat business. Cover BOTH halves of the question; each carries marks.

questions.question: You are the new restaurant manager at a seafront hotel. The day team and night team blame each other for problems, new starters are ignored, and three waiters have resigned this year. Produce a maximum of two training slides for the owner: the measures you will introduce to build positive working relationships, and the benefits these measures will bring to the business.
questions.model_answer: This mirrors the sample Scenario 3, so answer in the same shape: two slide- style bullet lists, nothing else. Model answer: Slide 1, Building the team: daily team briefings; a getting-to-know-you session with the whole team; mentoring and shadowing for every new starter; mixing staff across day and night shifts; a reward programme (star of the month) with praise by name; occasional social events. Slide 2, Benefits to the business: lower staff turnover, saving recruitment and training costs; higher productivity and increased sales; fewer mistakes and less waste; a professional image that earns good reviews and repeat business; a happy environment that attracts better staff. Format carries marks: slides, not paragraphs.

questions.question: At Spice Garden restaurant, chef Naseem constantly mocks a younger colleague, Raza. Raza has become withdrawn and is making mistakes. A quiet word from the supervisor changed nothing. Describe the further steps the business should take to deal with this situation, in the correct order.
questions.model_answer: The command is "describe... in the correct order", so the escalation ladder IS the mark scheme. Model answer shape: The informal step has failed, so the manager should formally involve HR, since repeated mocking is bullying (steps 1-2). HR investigates, hearing both sides fairly (step 3). If upheld, the formal disciplinary procedure applies, starting with a written warning (step 4). Mediation with a neutral person can rebuild the working relationship (step 5). Finally the business should set clear behaviour expectations and train the team, and follow up to check Raza is supported (step 6). Each correctly-ordered step with a line of detail earns its mark.

questions.question: You manage a cafe where all five staff are confident and quick, but orders keep going out wrong, everyone competes for the same jobs, and arguments break out daily. Produce a short guidance document for the owner: define team dynamics, explain why this team is struggling, and describe how you would use an understanding of team dynamics to improve performance.
questions.model_answer: SCAN, delivered as a headed guidance document because that's the format asked for. Spot: a team of similar personalities with no checkers or peacemakers, unclear roles. Cite: the definition of team dynamics (word for word) and "balanced teams outperform teams of similar people". Apply: observe the team to identify each person's strengths; assign clear roles (one leader at the pass, a careful person checking orders); rotate tasks weekly so every job is understood and respected. Name the outcome: fewer mistakes, fewer arguments, better service and returning customers. Model answer opening, exam-ready prose: "Team dynamics means the way team members' personalities, roles and relationships affect how the team behaves and performs. This cafe struggles because every member has a similar, dominant personality, so the team has five leaders and no checkers or peacemakers, and balanced teams outperform teams of similar people."

questions.question: Two receptionists at the Hilltop Hotel, Sara and Mahnoor, have stopped speaking to each other. Guests have noticed the frosty atmosphere at check-in. The cause appears to be confusion over whose job it is to handle group bookings. Describe how the hotel manager should manage this conflict, and explain how the business could prevent similar conflicts in future.
questions.model_answer: Walk the 8 steps in order; the "prevent" half of the question maps to step 8 and must not be skipped. Model answer skeleton: Spot and act now, before guests see more (1.). Speak away from the front desk, calmly (2.). Listen to Sara and Mahnoor separately and fairly (3.). Identify the real cause: unclear job roles over group bookings, not personal dislike (4.). Agree together who owns group bookings, in writing (5.). Follow up in two weeks (6.). If it continues, escalate to senior management or HR (7.). Prevent repeats with written job descriptions, fair workload allocation and regular team briefings (8.). Close with the outcome: professional check- ins, protected reputation.

questions.question: The owner of a busy kabab house knows his two senior cooks have not spoken to each other for three months, but says staff quarrels are "not his problem". You are a consultant hired by his family. Produce a short report for the owner: assess the impact this unresolved conflict could have on his business, and recommend the steps he should take to resolve it.
questions.model_answer: SCAN, in report format with two headed sections because that's the document asked for. Spot: a long-running, ignored conflict between key staff. Cite: the impact list and the 8- step sequence. Apply, section 1 (impacts): customers sense the atmosphere and stop returning; mistakes and waste rise because the cooks won't communicate; other staff are dragged in or resign, bringing recruitment and training costs; reviews damage the reputation; his own time drains into disputes; in the worst case a grievance or tribunal claim brings legal costs. Apply, section 2 (resolution): act now, away from the kitchen (1.2.); hear each cook separately and fairly (3.); dig for the real cause beneath the quarrel (4.); agree a written solution together (5.); follow up weekly (6.); escalate to formal procedures only if it continues (7.); prevent repeats with clear roles, fair hours and regular briefings (8.). Name the outcome: costs stop bleeding, the team stabilises, customers return. Model closing line, exam-ready prose: "Unresolved conflict is never free; acting early costs the owner an hour, while waiting costs him customers, staff and possibly a tribunal claim."

questions.question: An EHO inspects the Riverside Café and finds: no staff training records, a broken fridge running at 12°C, raw chicken stored above desserts, and a chef working two days after a stomach illness. Assess the possible consequences for the business and for the chef if these failures are not corrected.
questions.model_answer: SCAN, and "assess" means consequences carry the weight. Spot each failure and Cite the broken rule: no training records (operator duty), 12°C is inside the danger zone, raw above ready-to-eat = cross-contamination, and staff must stay off until 48 hours symptom-free. Apply: customers could be poisoned by Salmonella or Campylobacter from the chicken, or by the ill chef spreading bacteria. Name the outcomes, both sides: the operator faces improvement or prohibition notices, emergency closure, unlimited fines, a public low rating and compensation claims; the chef faces disciplinary action, dismissal, even personal prosecution. Judgement line: these failures risk lives, so the EHO could close the café immediately.

questions.question: (new) You have just been appointed manager of a small hotel restaurant with no food safety paperwork at all. Produce a short guidance document for the owner setting out (i) four things you will put in place to meet the operator's legal duties, and (ii) the consequences the business faces if you do not.
questions.model_answer: Paper 2-A rewards format, so use two headed sections and bullets, not an essay. Section (i) What we will put in place: a HACCP-based food safety management system covering delivery, storage, preparation, cooking and service; staff hygiene training with signed and dated records; temperature logs for every fridge and freezer plus calibrated probes; and controlled suppliers, pest control and a displayed allergen chart covering the 14 FSA allergens. Section (ii) Consequences of failure: customers made seriously ill or killed; an improvement notice, prohibition notice or emergency closure from the EHO; prosecution with unlimited fines and possible imprisonment; a low hygiene rating displayed publicly; compensation claims and higher insurance; and lasting damage to the hotel's name. Finish with one judgement line: the cost of the system is small next to the cost of one outbreak.

questions.question: At the end of service, chef Bina has a large pot of hot curry left over. She puts the steaming pot straight into the fridge, unlabelled, on the bottom shelf under nothing, with raw fish on the shelf above it. Describe the mistakes Bina has made and explain the correct procedure for storing this leftover curry.
questions.model_answer: SCAN; marks split between mistakes and correct procedure, so give both. Model answer: Bina refrigerated steaming food, which warms the whole fridge into the danger zone; she failed to label it; and she stored raw fish above cooked food, risking drips and cross- contamination (Spot + Cite). Correctly, she should divide the curry into shallow containers, cool it within 90 minutes, cover it, label it with contents and date, and store it above raw foods; it must be used within 2-3 days and reheated only once to 75°C or above (Apply). Done right, the curry stays safe to sell and no guest is put at risk (Name the outcome).

questions.question: (new) You are a supervisor at a banqueting kitchen. After a large wedding, your night cook must store several dishes and prepare commodities for the next day. Produce a short briefing sheet covering (i) the correct procedure for storing the leftover food overnight, and (ii) two preparation rules for poultry and two for shellfish that the cook must follow the next morning.
questions.model_answer: Paper 2-A rewards format, so answer as a briefing sheet with two headed sections and bullets. (i) Storing leftovers: divide into shallow containers, stand in cold water and stir; cool within 90 minutes, never put steaming food into the fridge; cover or seal; label with contents and date; store cooked above raw; fridge at 0-5°C, freezer at -18°C; use within 2-3 days; reheat once only to 75°C; if in doubt, throw it out. (ii) Poultry: never wash the bird because it splashes bacteria, and wash hands and surfaces after handling it; truss or joint it and marinate it in the fridge, never on the counter. (ii) Shellfish: keep mussels, prawns and lobster alive or chilled until cooking, and de-beard mussels, discarding any shell that is open or damaged and will not close when tapped. Close with one outcome line: following this sheet keeps every dish out of the danger zone and protects guests, staff and the hotel's hygiene rating.

questions.question: At a hotel buffet, waiter Imad notices the curry has been sitting on a broken hot-plate for an unknown time and now feels lukewarm. The chef tells him to "turn the heat up and serve it anyway; it was cooked to 75°C this morning." Assess whether the chef's instruction is safe, and describe what should be done instead.
questions.model_answer: SCAN with a firm judgement. Spot: lukewarm curry, unknown time below holding temperature. Cite: hot food must be held at 63°C or above; below that it sits in the 5- 63°C danger zone where bacteria such as Clostridium perfringens multiply, and reaching 75°C this morning does not undo hours of later growth (some bacteria produce heat-resistant toxins). Apply: the chef cannot know how long the curry was unsafe, so reheating "to look hot" does not make it safe. Name the outcome: serving it risks mass food poisoning, EHO action and the hotel's reputation; the curry should be discarded, the hot-plate repaired, and holding temperatures logged. Judgement: the instruction is unsafe and Imad should refuse and report it.

questions.question: (new) You are the chef running a Sunday carvery for 200 covers. Produce a short guidance sheet for a new commis chef covering (i) how the meats will be cooked and checked before service, (ii) how they will be held safely during the three-hour service, and (iii) what happens to any cooked meat left at the end.
questions.model_answer: three headed sections, bullets, numbers everywhere. (i) Cooking and checking: joints roasted in the oven at 170-185°C with fat spooned over the meat; every joint probed in the thickest part with a clean calibrated probe; a core reading of 75°C or above before it leaves the kitchen; poultry always cooked right through, never pink. (ii) Holding: hot-hold at 63°C or above under working lamps; probe every joint every 30 minutes and record the reading and the time; if any reading is below 63°C, or falling towards it, report to the head chef immediately and withdraw the joint, because food below 63°C is in the 5-63°C danger zone. (iii) End of service: do not reheat and re-serve mishandled food, since reheating cannot destroy toxins already produced; slice remaining sound joints thin onto shallow trays and cool them within 90 minutes, using a blast chiller where available; then cover, label and date, store in a fridge at 0-5°C above raw foods, use within 2-3 days and reheat once only to 75°C. Close with the judgement line: if the holding log has a gap or a doubt in it, the food is thrown away.

questions.question: A school canteen manager plans a lunch menu using only cured meats and white bread, because "they keep the longest". Assess the nutritional weaknesses of this plan and suggest improvements using your knowledge of food groups and preservation.
questions.model_answer: SCAN. Spot: one food group, heavily cured. Cite: cured meats are high in salt (blood pressure); a balanced diet needs all groups; freezing and canning can preserve food with better nutrition. Apply: add frozen vegetables (nutrients kept), canned fish like tuna (protein, convenience), fresh or frozen fruit, and lean poultry. Name the outcome: students get protein, vitamins, minerals and fibre, reducing deficiency risks, while the kitchen still gets long shelf life. Judgement: shelf life and nutrition are not enemies; frozen and canned choices give both.

questions.question: Nusrat manages the front desk team at a busy city hotel. Her staff work long shifts, seem stressed and tired, and several have made booking mistakes recently. Two younger staff are new to the city and know few people outside work. Nusrat plans a weekly staff cricket match and a lunchtime walking group. Assess how her plan could benefit her staff and the hotel.
questions.model_answer: SCAN. Spot: stress, tiredness, mistakes, and loneliness in the team. Cite: exercise releases endorphins and reduces stress and anxiety; it improves sleep, concentration and memory; team sport gives social contact that reduces loneliness and builds confidence. Apply: the walking group burns off shift stress and helps staff sleep, so booking errors from tired minds should fall; the cricket match gives the two newcomers a circle of friends inside the team. Name the outcome: calmer, sharper, better-connected staff make fewer mistakes and serve guests better, so the hotel benefits along with them. Judgement: a low-cost plan that targets every problem she spotted; the mind benefits of exercise are exactly what this team lacks.

questions.question: Danyal, aged 16, eats large amounts of fried food and sugary drinks but trains hard at the gym daily, saying "training cancels out my diet". His energy crashes in the afternoons and his progress has stopped. Assess Danyal's belief, and explain how a balanced diet and regular exercise work together to improve health.
questions.model_answer: SCAN with a clear judgement on the belief. Spot: Danyal treats exercise as a licence for poor eating. Cite: food is fuel and exercise is how the body uses it; energy balance means calories in vs calories out; protein repairs trained muscle; exercise cannot fix a poor diet. Apply: his fried, sugary fuel gives energy spikes and crashes and little protein for muscle repair, so training stalls despite effort. Name the outcome: swapping to balanced meals with protein, vegetables and water restores steady energy, lets muscles rebuild, and lowers long-term risks of obesity, heart disease and diabetes. Judgement: his belief is false; diet and exercise are partners, and one cannot replace the other.
